text: Gravatar's docs (checked October 2026) say to trim leading and trailing whitespace from the email, lowercase it, and hash it with SHA-256. Skipping the trim or lowercase step gives a different hash, so the avatar is not found.
why: Readers implementing the URL need the exact normalisation and current algorithm.

text: The avatar URL accepts parameters: s= sets the size (1 to 2048 px, default 80), and d= picks what to show when no avatar exists (a built-in default, your own image URL, or d=404 to get an HTTP 404).
why: Shows how the real service handles sizes and missing avatars, tying into the on-demand resizing section.

text: Because Gravatar hashes are unsalted and fast, anyone can hash a list of candidate emails and match them against Gravatar URLs, so guessable addresses can be identified. Solar Designer notes that switching from MD5 to SHA-256 is 'almost no change' for this.
why: Corrects the impression that hashing alone protects the email.

text: PostgreSQL can index an expression, e.g. CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email)); a query with WHERE lower(email) = 'x' then runs as fast as a simple index lookup. The cost is that the expression is computed on every insert and most updates.
why: Shows the alternative to storing a derived column.

text: MySQL 8 supports functional key parts, e.g. CREATE INDEX idx ON t ((col1 + col2)). The index is used only when the WHERE clause contains the same expression.
why: Same alternative for MySQL users.

text: In PostgreSQL's default Read Committed level, an UPDATE finds its target rows using a snapshot taken at the start of the statement. Two concurrent mark-active transactions can each clear only the old active row and then activate different photos, leaving two active. Lock the user's row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or keep a single active_photo_id on users.
why: Shows concretely why atomicity is not the same as concurrency safety.

text: The MySQL manual warns that a regular SELECT in a transaction 'does not give enough protection': other transactions can update or delete the rows you just read. Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (or FOR SHARE) so the checked row stays locked until COMMIT.
why: Makes the check-then-write pattern actually safe.

text: An UPDATE that matches no rows is not an error. In MySQL, ROW_COUNT() after an UPDATE returns the number of rows actually changed, so the application can check it and issue ROLLBACK when the count is 0.
why: Gives the concrete way to detect the 'nothing updated' alarm.

text: The step-by-step narrowing needs an index on photos.user_id. MySQL InnoDB creates an index on a foreign-key column automatically if none exists; PostgreSQL does not, and its docs say indexing the referencing column is often a good idea.
why: A common real-world miss when porting this schema to PostgreSQL.

text: MySQL converts a LEFT JOIN into an inner join when the WHERE condition is null-rejected (it can never be true for a NULL-filled row), as with photos.is_active = true. The rewrite frees the optimizer to pick a better join order.
why: Explains why the two joins perform the same here.

text: CloudFront Origin Access Control lets the CDN read a private S3 bucket by signing its requests. The bucket policy allows only that distribution, so viewers cannot use S3 URLs directly.
why: Corrects the 'S3 is not public' reason.

text: DNS does not allow a plain CNAME at the zone apex (gravatar.com). Using the root domain as a CDN hostname needs provider support such as Cloudflare's CNAME flattening, which answers with the target's IP addresses instead.
why: Practical catch when making the root domain the CDN property.

text: CDN invalidation clears only the CDN's edge caches: a browser or corporate proxy can keep showing the old file until its own copy expires. CloudFront recommends versioned file names for frequently updated files, and invalidations can cost money while versioning does not.
why: Sets expectations for 'immediately everywhere' after a photo change.

text: Cloudflare's docs recommend single-file purge (by URL) as the main purge method. It is available on every plan, with rate limits (e.g. 800 URLs per second on Free).
why: Grounds the 'every CDN has an invalidation API' claim in a real API.

text: Pillow, the maintained fork of PIL, has its own resize API (Image.resize). ImageMagick is used from Python through the separate Wand package, a ctypes-based binding that requires the MagickWand library.
why: Gives readers the right library names.

text: Cloudflare Images transforms images on the fly from URL parameters (resize, crop, convert to WebP/AVIF), with 'no pre-generated variants needed'.
why: A concrete example of the CDN feature the design re-implements.

text: Cloudflare's engineering blog says its Image Resizing service was developed in Rust, with its own processing and compression components, rather than built on ImageMagick.
why: Prevents readers attributing the anecdote to Cloudflare's current product.

text: In MySQL, BOOL is a synonym for TINYINT(1); the (1) is only a display width, so the column can actually hold any value from -128 to 127. Add a CHECK constraint if only 0/1 should be allowed.
why: Common surprise when using BOOL in MySQL.

text: PostgreSQL has no TINYINT: its smallest integer type is smallint (2 bytes). A 1-byte state column there is boolean, or use smallint with a CHECK constraint.
why: The advice is MySQL-specific; PostgreSQL readers need the equivalent.

text: MySQL starts each connection with autocommit enabled: it commits after every statement that does not return an error. Use START TRANSACTION ... COMMIT to group several statements into one transaction.
why: Pins down the 'single query is a transaction' claim.
